newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Metals markets slip as speculators sell.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Metals markets slip as speculators sell.

text.p: Metals markets spiralled lower on Monday, overwhelmed by gloomy sentiment as speculators battered prices once again.

Aluminium tumbled to a fresh 2-1/4-year low, tin touched a six-month nadir and copper, flagship of the industrial metals, slid further below a key level of support, although it found some support late in the day..
"The whole thing looks very sloppy indeed," said one floor trader on the London Metal Exchange (LME). "It's difficult to see when all this is going to end."
The precious metals were just as disspirited.
Platinum and palladium took their turn to take the brunt of the attack after silver led the complex down last week. Gold held its composure, but only just.
More weakness among the rest of the precious complex could soon push gold over the edge to fresh lows for 1996, analysts said.

It was a far cry from blistering rallies earlier in the year, which took gold to six-year highs near $418 per ounce and emboldened some to talk of a new bull market in industrial metals fuelled by roaring global economic growth.
But in many regions economic growth has been lacklustre while US stock markets have continued surging, drawing attention and money away from commodity markets.
Large US investment funds unleashed more selling on the LME on Monday, pushing aluminium under the important $1,400 benchmark, an area the metal has not seen since June 1994.
Aluminium for three months delivery ended the day at $1,392, shedding $20 from Friday, compared to a high in January near $1,700.
Rising production and inventories together with sluggish global offtake were pressuring prices, analysts said.

Tin also saw the floor fall out from under it, tumbling nearly $100 to settle at midday at $6,010 per tonne, the weakest price since March this year. It edged up slightly at the afternoon close to $6,030.
Traders said comments by a Brazilian trade official that world tin stocks would finish 1996 at 36,000 tonnes against 30,000 at the end of 1995 weighed on the market.

Copper, the most activiely traded of the industrial metals, continued to erode lower after losing grip of the key $1,900 level late on Friday. It ended the morning down $33 at $1,867 before staging an afternoon rally to close at $1,883..

The market peaked at $2,715 in May, but is starting to feel the weight of growing output from new mines, which is expected to accelerate in 1997, and speculators are taking advantage of the weakness, analysts said.
Speculators also kept up the pressure on the precious metals complex.
Platinum fixed at $386.50 per ounce, the lowest level in nearly 2-1/4 years as steady sales from major producer Russia eroded confidence since the summer when prices were above $400.
Sharp losses in silver last week spread a chill throughout the precious metals.
"The mood is not good," said one European analyst, adding that one US fund was said to have sold 40 million ounces of silver last week.
Platinum's stablemate palladium crumbled to fresh three-year lows, fixing at $116.75 per ounce, down from $122 last week.
Gold was teetering on the edge of the key $380 level, but improved Far Eastern jewellery demand was helping steady prices.
World barley markets were holding steady while attention was being focused on the emerging details of a huge 1.4 million tonnes purchase by Saudi Arabia, an influential importer.
